title: Subsets
description: Brute force to optimized: recursive include/exclude backtracking versus direct bitmask enumeration.

blocks.text: Like listing every possible pizza order from a fixed set of toppings, where each topping is either included or left off, and every combination of choices, including no toppings at all, counts as one valid order.

blocks.caption: Every element is either included or excluded, generating every possible combination

blocks.text: Edge case: nums with no elements (conceptually, an empty array)
An empty array has exactly one subset, the empty subset itself, giving [[]].
Before writing any code, notice what actually varies from one subset to the next: not the elements themselves, but the yes-or-no decision made independently for each one.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every element in nums has exactly two possible states inside any subset, present or absent.

Observation 2: With n elements, there are exactly 2 to the power n ways to assign those states, since each element's choice is independent of every other element's choice.

Observation 3: A recursive include/exclude walk down the array visits precisely these 2 to the power n leaf combinations, one per completed decision path.

Observation 4: Those same 2 to the power n combinations are exactly the binary numbers from 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1, where each bit position says whether the corresponding element is present.

The moment a problem says "every combination of independent yes or no choices," think bitmask: count in binary from 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1 and read off which elements each number turns on.

This is why the same problem can be solved by two seemingly different techniques, recursive backtracking and bitmask iteration: they are walking over the exact same 2 to the power n outcomes, just in a different order and with a different mechanism for tracking the decisions made so far.
Recursively build every subset by deciding, one element at a time, whether to include it or exclude it, branching into both choices at each step.

items: Starting from an empty current subset and index 0, at every element make two recursive calls, one including the current element and one excluding it.
Once every element has been decided, record the completed subset.

codes.python:
def subsets(nums):
    result = []

    def backtrack(index, current):
        if index == len(nums):
            result.append(current[:])
            return
        backtrack(index + 1, current)                            # exclude this element
        current.append(nums[index])
        backtrack(index + 1, current)                             # include this element
        current.pop()

    backtrack(0, [])
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: backtrack is called twice at every index, once choosing to exclude the current element and once choosing to include it, so both branches of the decision tree are explored completely.

current.append/current.push_back runs immediately before the include call, and current.pop()/current.pop_back() runs immediately after it, mutating one shared list in place and undoing the change afterward, which avoids copying the list at every recursive call.

The base case index == len(nums) is where a completed subset is copied into result using current[:] / new ArrayList<>(current) / current, since current itself keeps changing as the recursion continues to unwind and explore other branches.

blocks.text: Every element's two possibilities, included or excluded, are explored at every level, so every one of the 2 to the power n subsets is correctly generated exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times 2 to the power n), since there are 2 to the power n subsets, each up to length n to copy into the result.
Space: O(n), for the recursion stack depth.

Limitation: this is already essentially optimal in terms of complexity, since the output itself requires generating 2 to the power n subsets. The recursion, however, hides a direct correspondence: every subset corresponds exactly to one binary number from 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1, where each bit says whether that element is included.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The recursive solution already visits exactly 2 to the power n leaves, so there is no way to reduce the count of subsets produced, the work is asymptotically optimal already. What can change is how each leaf is reached. Recursion tracks the current partial subset explicitly, pushing and popping elements onto a shared list, and pays a function call and stack cost per decision. If the decisions themselves are just bits, they can be represented directly as one integer, and that integer's own binary form already encodes the full decision path taken to reach it. Counting from 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1 in order therefore visits the exact same 2 to the power n decision paths as recursion, but reads them off arithmetically instead of tracking them through a call stack.

Instead of a recursive include/exclude decision tree, iterate directly over every integer from 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1. Each such integer's binary representation is a bitmask: bit i being set means element i is included in that subset. Reading off the set bits of each number directly produces the corresponding subset, without any recursive call stack at all.
Iterate over every bitmask from 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1, reading off which elements each one includes.

blocks.caption: Optimized: every bitmask from 0 to 2^n minus 1 directly encodes one subset

codes.python:
def subsets(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    result = []
    for mask in range(1 << n):                                # every number from 0 to 2^n minus 1
        current = []
        for i in range(n):
            if mask & (1 << i):                                     # check whether bit i is set in this mask
                current.append(nums[i])
        result.append(current)
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times 2 to the power n), the same as the recursive version, since this is the true size of the output.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the output, since no recursion stack is used at all.

Each of the n bits in a mask is an independent yes-or-no flag for one specific element, so the n-bit binary numbers from 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1 enumerate every combination of flags exactly once, with nothing duplicated and nothing missed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bit position","If set (1)","If unset (0)"],"rows":[["Bit 0","nums[0] is included in the current subset","nums[0] is excluded from the current subset"],["Bit 1","nums[1] is included in the current subset","nums[1] is excluded from the current subset"],["Bit 2","nums[2] is included in the current subset","nums[2] is excluded from the current subset"]]}

items: 1 << n computes 2 to the power n, the total number of subsets, so the outer loop's mask runs across every integer in that full range exactly once.
The inner loop checks mask & (1 << i) for every bit position i from 0 to n minus 1, which isolates just that one bit and tests whether it is set.
Every time a bit is found set, the corresponding nums[i] is appended to the current subset being built for that mask.
Once all n bits have been checked, current holds exactly the subset that mask encodes, and it is appended to result.

blocks.text: This problem is the direct bridge between recursion based include/exclude decisions and bitmask enumeration: every leaf of the recursive decision tree corresponds to exactly one binary number, and recognizing that correspondence is what places this problem naturally in the bit manipulation category rather than purely under backtracking.

items: Assuming the bitmask approach is asymptotically faster than the recursive one: both are already bound by the same unavoidable 2 to the power n output size, so the real benefit is avoiding recursion overhead, not reaching a better complexity class.

Getting the bit index and the element index mixed up, checking the wrong bit for a given element position: this silently produces the wrong subset for that mask instead of throwing an error, since both remain valid array indices.
Getting the loop bound wrong for the mask, an off-by-one either misses the full subset with all bits set or misses the empty subset at mask 0.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Return all possible subsets" or "every way to choose elements from a set" points to power set enumeration, solvable by either recursive include/exclude backtracking or bitmask iteration over 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1.

items: What if nums can contain duplicates? Sort the array first and skip duplicate branches at the same recursion depth to avoid producing duplicate subsets.
Can you generate only subsets of a fixed size k? Restrict the recursion depth, or restrict the bitmask to only those values whose set-bit count equals k.
How would you generate subsets without holding all of them in memory at once? Yield or print each subset as it is generated instead of collecting every one into a result list.
Same include/exclude recursion structure as 0/1 Knapsack and Combination Sum, just without a target sum constraint pruning the branches.
Same bitmask enumeration technique used in subset-based dynamic programming (such as Traveling Salesman style DP) and in counting problems over every subset of a small set.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force (recursive include/exclude): O(n times 2 to the power n) time, O(n) recursion stack space.
Optimized (bitmask iteration): O(n times 2 to the power n) time, O(1) extra space beyond the output.

items: Pattern: Power set enumeration via include/exclude recursion or bitmask iteration
Core Idea: Every subset corresponds to exactly one binary number from 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1
Time: O(n times 2 to the power n)
Space: O(n) recursion stack for the brute force, O(1) extra for the bitmask version
Most Important Observation: n independent yes-or-no choices produce exactly 2 to the power n outcomes, whether reached through recursion or by counting in binary
Interview Difficulty: Easy to Medium
One-line memory trick: Every subset is a binary number in disguise
